introduction_markdown:
This paper is arranged in three sections, A, B and C. Section A: answer ALL 5 questions; you will be graded for the best 4 answers. Section B: answer ALL 2 questions in this section. Section C: answer 2 questions out of 3; if you attempt more than 2 questions, only the first two will be considered. In calculations, you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. Calculators are allowed. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

**Useful data:** relative atomic masses H = 1.0, C = 12.0, O = 16.0, N = 14.0; 1 faraday = 96000 coulombs; molar volume of a gas at r.t.p. = 24000 cm$^3$; specific heat capacity of water = 4.2 J g$^{-1}$ $^\circ$C$^{-1}$; Avogadro number = $6.02\times10^{23}$; $0^\circ$C = 273 K.
incertitudes: Points imprimés « (4, 16 marks) » = 20, conformes ; la première partie (a) vaut 4 et la seconde (b) 16. Le choix des quatre facteurs et des quatre réactions (magnésium + acide, thiosulfate + acide, marbre + acide, eau oxygénée + MnO2) est une réponse modèle parmi d'autres acceptables.

En-tête de la Section A : « ANSWER ALL 5 questions. You will be graded for the best 4 answers » ; modélisé en « 4 sur 5 » (toutes tentées, 4 meilleures notées). Section B : « ANSWER ALL 2 questions » modélisé en « 2 sur 2 ». Section C : « ANSWER 2 QUESTIONS OUT OF 3 » (si plus de 2 tentées, seules les deux premières comptent) ; modélisé en « 2 sur 3 ».

questions.enonce_markdown: List four factors which affect the rate of chemical reactions. *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
1. **Concentration** of the reacting solutions (or **pressure** for gases).
2. **Temperature**.
3. **Surface area** (particle size) of a solid reactant.
4. **Presence of a catalyst**.

(Light is a fifth factor for some reactions, for example the decomposition of silver salts.)

questions.enonce_markdown: Using a suitable chemical reaction for each factor, describe how the factor affects the rate of the chemical reactions. *[16 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
All the factors are explained by **collision theory**: a reaction happens when particles collide with enough energy (the activation energy), and the rate depends on the number of effective collisions per second.

**1. Concentration** - reaction of magnesium with dilute hydrochloric acid: $\mathrm{Mg(s)} + 2\mathrm{HCl(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{MgCl_2(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2(g)}$.
Equal strips of magnesium ribbon are added to HCl of different concentrations (for example 0.5, 1.0 and 2.0 mol dm$^{-3}$) at the same temperature, and the volume of hydrogen is collected in a gas syringe against time. **Observation:** the more concentrated the acid, the more rapid the fizzing and the shorter the time to collect a given volume. **Explanation:** more acid particles per unit volume, so more frequent collisions with magnesium and a higher rate.

**2. Temperature** - reaction of sodium thiosulphate with dilute hydrochloric acid: $\mathrm{Na_2S_2O_3(aq)} + 2\mathrm{HCl(aq)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NaCl(aq)} + \mathrm{S(s)} + \mathrm{SO_2(g)} + \mathrm{H_2O(l)}$.
The mixture is made in a flask on a cross drawn on paper; the time for the cross to disappear (because of the yellow sulphur precipitate) is measured at different temperatures (for example 20, 30, 40, 50 $^\circ$C). **Observation:** the higher the temperature, the shorter the time, so the faster the reaction (roughly doubling for each $10^\circ$C rise). **Explanation:** the particles move faster, collide more often and a larger fraction of collisions have energy at least equal to the activation energy.

**3. Surface area** - reaction of marble (calcium carbonate) with dilute hydrochloric acid: $\mathrm{CaCO_3(s)} + 2\mathrm{HCl(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaCl_2(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2O(l)} + \mathrm{CO_2(g)}$.
The same mass of marble is used once as large lumps and once as powder, with the same acid at the same temperature, and the loss in mass (or the volume of $\mathrm{CO_2}$) is measured with time. **Observation:** the powder reacts much faster (vigorous fizzing, finished sooner) than the lumps. **Explanation:** the powder exposes a larger surface area, so more particles of the solid are in contact with the acid, giving more collisions per second.

**4. Catalyst** - decomposition of hydrogen peroxide: $2\mathrm{H_2O_2(aq)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)}$.
Hydrogen peroxide decomposes very slowly by itself; when a little manganese(IV) oxide, $\mathrm{MnO_2}$, is added, oxygen is given off rapidly (a glowing splint relights). **Observation:** the manganese(IV) oxide is unchanged in mass at the end. **Explanation:** the catalyst provides another pathway with a **lower activation energy**, so a larger fraction of collisions are effective; it is not used up.
